speechtext:
Following three such eminent speakers and astute politicians I am in rather a difficult position if I am to make any showing whatever. I should like to begin my few remarks in support of this resolution by congratulating the mover of the resolution (Mr. Speakman), on the general terms in which it has been worded. Again I would congratulate him upon the very reasonable way in which he explained the purport of the resolution. On the other hand, I was surprised at the attitude taken by the Minister of Trade and Commerce (Mr. Stevens). Particularly, the minister stressed the remarks in reference to soviet Russia made by my hon. friend the member for Winnipeg North Centre (Mr. Woodsworth). I was greatly surprised at the remarks of the minister in view of the fact that the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre definitely stated when making reference to Russia that he was drawing attention to that country only to show what could be done by organized planning. I cannot see any particular harm in that. The fact of the matter is that, whether we wish to admit it or not, at the present time the eyes of .the world are focused on Russia. A few weeks ago Sir Frederick Williams Taylor on his return from Europe made the following statement to the press: " Keep your eyes on Russia." Following the return of the Minister of Trade and Commerce from Europe after the Imperial economic conference last fall the Vancouver Sun contained an interview. This article is dated Ottawa, December 31, 1930, and is as follows:
Declaring that Russia's five-year plan was succeeding all along the line and that Canadians were doing their country a distinct disservice by pretending otherwise, Hon. H. H. Stevens .Minister of Trade and Commerce, arrived here at noon to-day after two months m London attending the Imperial conference.
Air. htevens is persuaded that one of the biggest economic problems for the world and tor Canada to consider is that presented by the steady come-back of soviet Russia, which was buying incredibly large quantities of goods in the United Kingdom and in the United States and paying for them.

I suppose the peculiar part about it is that she was paying for them. Then the interview continues:
As an exporter, Russia, which is in the same latitude as Canada, can and does sell practically all of the natural products as Canada, and soon will also be selling many of the articles that Canada manufactures and exports.
Russia will soon be a live competitor oi Canada, not only in wheat and coal but in many of the Dominion's other main commodities.
It is not surprising that my hon. friend from Winnipeg North Centre should have referred to Russia when the Minister of Trade and Commerce made reference in the terms I have quoted. The resolution in my opinion merely emphasizes the philosophy of most hon. members in the particular group to which I belong. In this Dominion there are various schools of thought which advocate the carrying on and organizing of the nation's business along various lines. As everybody knows the Labour group believes in the evolutionary process in human society. Consequently when we see an evolutionary process taking place and reaching the stage where a crisis is imminent we believe some steps should be taken to meet such a situation.
May I endeavour to illustrate my thoughts in this way? All hon. members who have had any experience in raising poultry will know that if fertile eggs are secured, put into an incubator and subjected to a heat approximating 103 degrees, at the end of twenty-one days baby chicks will hatch. The Labour party feels that is the way human society should go. Our friends the communists, who are in favour of a revolution, believe that if you increased the heat a few more degrees you might get the chicks in fifteen days, but the only thing that would really happen would be that you would cook the eggs. My friends the conservatives-and I do not mean the party but those people of a conservative type of mind as exemplified possibly by my hon. friend the Minister of Trade and Commerce (Mr. Stevens), believe that you can keep those chicks alive in the eggs after the twenty-one days are over, or if not, that possibly you could catch them and put them back in the shell after they came out. We believe that conditions are progressing towards a crisis in society, and just as you would prepare your brooder houses and other apparatus in order to care for your chicks, we believe it is the primary function of the government to prepare for contingencies, not only those which are already here but those which may arise later.

Economic Research-Mr. Maclnnis
If there is anything which is outstanding in connection with our present economic crisis it is, if I may use the term, the unanimous confusion of thought in regard to what causes it. I have gathered from various sources the opinions of many people who are supposed to be leaders in our industrial, financial and other activities to-day. I will give a list of those people and then I will give you their suggestions as to what has caused this world wide economic depression, together with their remedies for the situation. First there is Lord D'Abernon, famous British economist; J. M. Keynes, noted economist and chairman of the National Mutual Life Assurance Society of England; J. Beaumont Pease, chairman of Lloyd's Bank; Sir Harry Goschen, chairman, National Provincial Bank of London; Right Hon. Reginald McKenna; Harold Cox, noted British economist and writer; the financial expert of the London Times; J. F. Darling, director of the Midland Bank of England; Sir Herbert Holt, president of the Royal Bank of Canada, and several others. Some of the reasons given by these people for present economic conditions are: Gold hoarding by the United States and France; the unwillingness of the United States and France to make foreign loans; shortage of monetary gold, and inadequacy of world distributing machinery. I am unable to understand what that term really means. If it means the inadequacy of the medium of exchange, as far as the great masses of the people are concerned, I quite understand it, but if the word "machinery" means our transportation systems, then it has no meaning whatever.
Some further reasons given by prominent people are immobility of labour and interference of trade unions, and paternalist government. If there is any trade union at the moment which can interfere with the economic activities of the country, I should like to belong to that union. Other reasons are: disequilibrium of the gold standard; high prices of manufactured merchandise; tariff walls and anti-dumping measures; widening of the gap between wholesale and retail prices and interference with the easy flow of capital between countries. There seem to be just as many different causes as there were individuals giving them, but the point I wish to make is this: If gold hoarding by the United States and France is a cause, how did it come about that gold gravitated to those two countries? What caused the cause? If the inadequacy of world distributing machinery, using the word in the only sense in which it can be used, is a cause, what brought about
the inadequacy? This reminds me of a lecture I heard by a medical man, and after hearing my hon. friend from Wetaskiwin (Mr. Irvine) speak on this point I am not sure whether he was just as wise in this connection as he is in most of what he says. However, this medical gentleman, in giving an address on disease, said that rheumatism was caused by diseased tonsils and that heart disease was caused by rheumatism. He stopped there; he did not tell us what caused the diseased tonsils, and it is the same with these people. They tell us that the high prices of manufactured merchandise caused the present depression. Who is responsible for the high prices of manufactured merchandise? Is that not something which might be investigated by this committee?
Let us go on and recite a few more of the reasons given for the present economic depression. There was a gentleman from Great Britain who came over to this country not long ago; I refer to Sir Arthur Balfour, former president of the Federation of British Industries. Speaking at Hamilton, I believe, recently he is quoted as follows:
Sir Arthur Balfour noted that the world's population had increased by ten per cent in the period from 1923 to 1928. During the same period, however, he said that there had been an increase in agricultural production of sixteen per cent. The production of raw materials had increased thirty-five per cent, while the output of manufactured products had gone up forty per cent. You see,-he is reported as saying.-there are not enough people to consume the products.
I would imagine that such a statement was made by Sir Arthur Balfour after a very nice luncheon with people of his own kind. Certainly he could not meet a gathering of unemployed in any part of this Dominion and say there were not enough people to consume the products which were being manufactured. I believe this is something this research committee could investigate. Why is the condition of the people worse to-day than it was at any time between 1923 and 1928, when there has been an increase in agricultural products of sixteen per cent, in raw materials of thirty-five per cent and in manufactured products of forty per cent, with an increase in population of only ten per cent? It seems to me this is a problem for the research committee, that is, if the very efficient employees in the various government departments have not already investigated and reported on the matter.
Then we had another gentleman who came to this country at the request of the Dominion

Economic Research-Mr. Maclnnis
government to carry on an investigation. I refer to Sir Josiah Stamp. He is quoted as having said:
For Canada, a short wheat crop might prove an act of God which would start her forward again.
Surely here is a situation which someone or some organization should investigate. There is material enough here to keep this research council working for a great many days, I should think.
Now, I quote from a speech made by the Prime Minister on December 30 in the city of Regina, I believe. He said:
The marketing of the wheat crop will still leave our agriculturists without a sufficient competence for the winter months, which will find them when the spring comes without the seed for next year's crop. I cannot make up my mind why this country, between the lakes and the mountains, should experience the depression; why people who have lived here for years should now find themselves without any accumulation of goods, sometimes without the bare necessities of life.
With all this confusion, and all this want of understanding with regard to the distress that prevails in this Dominion to-day, is it not really time that some committee of the kind proposed in this resolution should be appointed? Is it not time that we established such a research council to investigate and try if possible to bring about a solution for our problems? That, I think, was in the mind of the Minister of Trade and Commerce (Mr. Stevens) when he spoke last year at the special session of parliament. At page 320 of Hansard of that special session I find the hon. gentleman reported in reference to a sug-* gestion made by the leader of the opposition (Mr. Mackenzie King) in connection with the return of people to the land as a solution for the problem of unemployment. The Minister of Trade and Commerce at that time said: For many years eastern Canada and the Pacific coast poured twenty or thirty thousand men annually into the western provinces during harvest time. Did any men go west for that purpose this year? The answer is that practically none went.
Mr. Vallance:	They rode in free.
Mr. Stevens:	Practically none went, and
they are riding out free also. Why?
Mr. Donnelly:	Because of the combines.
Mr. Stevens: Certainly, because of the introduction of modern machinery, combines and new harvesting machinery, which is doing away with the need for extra men. How then, in the face of this economic fact, can that solution mean anything? I jwould say to the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre (Mr. Woodsworth), who is not just now in his seat, that I think at some appropriate time the house can very well discuss this problem of the displacement of man power by machinery. 
Perhaps this is not the time, but it is an economic problem which is challenging the attention of the world, and I want to say now that it must have the attention of this parliament sooner or later. The fact is that machinery is displacing man power on the farms of the west, and whether the right hon. gentleman likes it or not, whether he puts his tariff on a free trade basis or not, these things are happening and will continue to happen and the men will have to go somewhere to get food.
I regard this, Mr. Speaker, as being in line with what we have suggested in this resolution. Let it be understood in the first place that, as the hon. member for Wetaskiwin (Mr. Irvine) has pointed out, this is only a fact-finding body. It does not offer a program nor evolve a policy for the government to follow. It would find facts in relation to various matters brought before it, and if these facts appeared reasonable I presume that action could be taken in correlating them with different activities in order to improve conditions. If it submitted such facts the government would no doubt be in a position to take action. But it would not be necessary that action should be taken unless the government felt satisfied that the information which was disclosed warranted it.
Within recent years considerable progress has been made along many lines, the effects of which we are now feeling. Speaking the other day, the Prime Minister said he could not understand how it was that everyone seemed to want the government to do this, that and the other thing in the way of social service. The fact is that with the industrial revolution, as the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre (Mr. Woodsworth) pointed out on Monday last, man was taken away from the land. About the year 1831, it was estimated that 90 per cent of the world's population were about that time living on the land, but when the industrial revolution came man was separated from the tools of production; and later on he was separated from his skill as a workman. Now he is not only separated from the tools of production and from his skill, but he is separated from the job itself by the automatic machine. Here, therefore, is a problem that needs to be met, a situation which would seem to come very well within the purview of such a council as has been suggested in the resolution of the hon. member for Red Deer (Mr. Speakman).
Speaking of the revolution that has occurred in agriculture, an interesting article appeared on October 30, 1930, in The Commerce of the Nation, written by Senator \\. A. Buchanan, which article I think is well

Economic Research-Air. Maclnnis
worthy the attention of all hon. members of this house. The hon. senator begins his article thus:
Western agriculture has undergone a revolution. Unemployment is the result. Canada is in the throes of the dislocation which accompanies all revolutions.
Following that, he discusses the operation of a section of land of 640 acres at Stirling. Alberta. He states:
During the past two years the owner has sown 320 acres to wheat, averaging more than 30 bushels to the acre-10,000 bushels of wheat each year. He has sown the wheat in the spring, has cultivated his summer-fallow for the next year's crop, has harvested the crop and hauled it to the elevator; and he has performed every operation without an hour's help. With liis own labour, and with the use of modern machinery, he has been able to operate a section of prairie wheat land, produce more than $10,000 worth of wheat each year, deliver it to the market and do every operation connected *with the task himself.
He goes on to examine all the labour-saving machinery on the farm. I do not wish to suggest for a moment that there has not been some employment in the production of that machinery. But the fact is that the mobilization of labour in any particular place by the use of machinery and motor-driven machinery is displacing labour much more quickly than we can at the present moment provide for.
At the special session of parliament last year we made an appropriation of $20,000,000 to take care of unemployment. A part of that $20,000,000 was made available to the two large railway companies to pay the carrying charges on certain purchases which they really did not need to make at the time, but which was made in order to relieve the unemployment situation. But while the treasury was making that contribution what were the railways themselves doing? A few days ago a friend of mine who is in a position to know told me .that where until recently 42 men were engaged in the Canadian National Railways Turcotte shop at Montreal in cleaning engines, through the introduction of machinery their number had been reduced to four. While we were thus helping the Canadian National Railways, the management, by the introduction of more modern labour-saving machinery, was displacing men possibly faster than we could take care of them. And the Canadian Pacific Railway has been doing pretty much the same thing. In the Vancouver gun of October 20, 1930, appears the following news item:
A revolutionary change in operating system is planned by the Canadian Pacific Railway throughout the west in the next few months.
Locomotives on passenger trains will carry their loads as far as 1,200 miles in one run, instead of about 125 miles as under the present divisional system, it is announced by Mr. W. M. Neal, general manager of western lines.
Time saved at divisional terminals, where it no longer will be necessary to change engines, and the saving of locomotive maintenance costs as well as in the reduced number of engines required are reasons for the change, Mr. Neal said.
The new system also will enable the railway company to make wider use of its latest and more powerful engines, now available in only limited numbers.
Decision to extend the long-run system from Fort William to Vancouver follows an experiment made by the Canadian Pacific Railway last spring, when an engine hauled a train 1,252 miles from Fort William to Calgary in scheduled time, and retraced this mileage with another train, also in scheduled time.
Under the new system it will be necessary to have only five motive power divisions against fourteen formerly in use, Mr. Neal pointed out. One engine, for example, will carry through from Fort William to Winnipeg; a second from Winnipeg to Calgary; a third from Calgary to Field; a fourth from Field to Revelstoke, and a fifth from Revelstoke to Vancouver.
Success of the long-run system already has been satisfactorily established on one district, where 30 engines now do the work of 51, Mr. Neal stated.
Surely in view of such conditions bringing about a still greater degree of unemployment, there is every reason for the establishment of a fact-finding organization to enable the government to plan and act intelligently.
Whether the government likes it or not, economic conditions are making it more necessary each year that it take a greater part in the economic life of the nation. This afternoon it was pointed out what the function of government has been in the past and what it is believed to be to-day, but that the government is not keeping pace with the times. We have not to go back vary far in history to find that in the British isles, where we get our pattern for parliamentary institutions, government at first was in the hands of the king and the barons, that the development of constitutional government was very gradual, and that it was not until quite recently that the working people came to take any part at all in governing the country, and consequently it is only since then that their interests have been given any consideration 'by those in authority. The function of government in England up to within recent years was to find "spheres of influence" and secure export markets for their manufactured commodities. Foreign trade was occasionally forced on reluctant nations by the aid of the army and navy, the militia was kept at home to look after the workers. That, I

Economic Research-Mr. Maclnnis
should say, until comparatively a few years ago was the prime function of government in Great Britain. To-day through the invention of labour-saving machinery more and more people are being out of employment and in every industrial country the government must of necessity take a closer and more active interest in the economic life of its people. The Minister of Trade and Commerce may say that already we are assisting research councils, but, I would remind him, these councils are not. working in the interests of the people at large, they are working in the interests of the various industrial corporations, and these are mainly concerned in making a profit for their shareholders; they have not got at heart the interests of this Dominion.

subsubtopic: MOTION BY MR. SPEAKMAN PROPOSING ESTABLISHMENT OF NATIONAL COUNCIL TO STUDY SUBJECT
speechtext: If the hon. gentleman will pardon me, I know he would not want to do a grave injustice to a very excellent institution which is only semi-governmental. He is entirely wrong in his statement.	.

subsubtopic: MOTION BY MR. SPEAKMAN PROPOSING ESTABLISHMENT OF NATIONAL COUNCIL TO STUDY SUBJECT
speechtext: In the way my hon. friend interprets my statement I may be wrong, but I submit that in fact I am not wrong. When the research bureau makes any discovery it is passed on to our various industrial concerns, and they use the information not for the good of the country, but for the profit of their shareholders.

subsubtopic: MOTION BY MR. SPEAKMAN PROPOSING ESTABLISHMENT OF NATIONAL COUNCIL TO STUDY SUBJECT
speechtext: That is not correct.

subsubtopic: MOTION BY MR. SPEAKMAN PROPOSING ESTABLISHMENT OF NATIONAL COUNCIL TO STUDY SUBJECT
speechtext:
If it is not correct I should like to know of one private organization whose shareholders are interested in forwarding the welfare of this country, that is, considering the country as an aggregation of individuals, and the welfare of each being given due consideration.
We all realize that we are going through critical times, As a matter of fact I think we all agree that possibly the government of Canada and the governments of the other countries of the world, have greater responsibilities to-day than ever before. I am quite sure that is true with respect to our federal government, and, speaking for the Labour section in this chamber, I say it is because we wish to help bring about the impending changes referred to with as little dislocation of industry and with as little suffering to the people as possible, that on every occasion possible we urge the government to take action and not wait until we have a crisis upon us that will possibly be altogether beyond our control. I am quite satisfied that that would not meet the wishes of some people, but it does agree with my views in regard to the 
proper organization of government. We have been twitted time and time again by speakers on the Conservative side of the house with not making suggestions, but it is rather strange that on the two occasions when we made specific suggestions, they were thrown back in our faces without any consideration whatsoever.

subsubtopic: MOTION BY MR. SPEAKMAN PROPOSING ESTABLISHMENT OF NATIONAL COUNCIL TO STUDY SUBJECT
speechtext:
I regret that the time at my disposal will hardly permit my analyzing the speeches that have already been .made in this debate. Let me, however, say at the outset that I regard the proposal of the hon. member for Red Deer (Mr. Speakman) as one of the most important that have been brought before the house in recent years. The proposal is not by any means a new one. It has been intimated time and time again in speeches made by hon. members in this corner of the house that a complete social and economic survey of this country is a vital necessity. It is answered by both the Minister of Trade and Commerce (Mr. Stevens) and the leader of the opposition [Mr. Mackenzie King), that a broad interpretation of the existing act under which the National Research Council is constituted, permits of the very thing that we are asking for in this resolution. Well and good. If that be true, then they indict and condemn themselves for their inactivity in this regard. If the possibility for a full investigation into the economic and social conditions in this country exists, as they admit and, in fact, insist it exists, and if they have not, as they also admit, undertaken that investigation, they stand condemned out of their own mouths.
Has this matter been drawn to their attention recently? No later than last April I had the privilege of speaking in the house on the problem of unemployment and all that it involves. The leader of the opposition referred to that to-day and he submitted that it was the government's present duty-he said it in almost those words-to submit this problem for solution to the National Research Council. Last April I made these few humble remarks myself:
I say to the Prime Minister-
He is now the leader of the opposition.
-that until he and his colleagues appoint a body to make a survey of economic and social conditions, a commission capable of intelligently analyzing this situation, he has not taken any step in the direction of a real solution of this problem.
Some months later the light dawned upon him and he now submits to the government that they have to refer this question to the National Research Council. This interpreta-

Economic Research-Mr. Garland (Bow River)
tion, belated, it is true, may be accurate. It may be correct that the National Research Council has the power to investigate these matters, but we have no evidence from any hon. member who has spoken so far in this debate, that any such question was ever at any time referred for examination, analysis, and solution, to any scientific body in the country. On the contrary, what do we find? We find in this country, one of the richest on earth, vast and illimitable resources to which people so glibly and eloquently refer both in election speeches and otherwise; we find a mechanical and technical equipment second to none in the world in proportion to our size and population; we find electrical energy in enormous quantity and of priceless value; we find a class of workmen who are skilled, energetic, adaptable, as able and intelligent as any class of workmen in any country and in any age. In view of this there is no sound reason why there should be any poverty in Canada. There is no sound reason why there should be any unemployment in this country, and I am almost quoting the words of the leader of the government during the last campaign when I say that. Every man and woman in this country willing to work should be able to lead a life not only of security but of comfort and plenty, and even have time to develop culture.
What is the case? What have we got? We have hunger and poverty around us in the capital city of Canada as well as in every other city. We have men and women discouraged with the struggle of trying to make a living under the adverse system under which we operate. We have .people whose morale is being destroyed by the disappointment of every day that comes upon them, people underfed and undernourished, people whose vitality is being lowered, whose whole future outlook on life is being affected. We have to-day a system which not only has not solved the problems that it should have solved but, on the contrary, is pressing a growing mass of the people into further and further destitution. All that the resolution asks this house is that a special scientific body of some kind be appointed to examine into this condition of affairs, find out the basic factors causing this condition, and offer solutions. This parliamentary institution is wholly unfitted for that kind of work. Hon. members have such multifarious, petty little duties to perform that the average member has no time to make an exhaustive examination into economic conditions, much less submit a proposition, and, as the hon. member for Wetaskiwin (Mr. Irvine) has said, often when
they are submitted to the house, they are discounted as coming from faddists and cranks. But I am sometimes reminded when you have not a self starter, you have to have a crank.
The view that parliament is not fitted to examine into and give intelligent consideration to the basic causes of conditions as we have them, or to provide solutions, is not confined to hon. members in this comer. Even such a well known world figure as the Right Hon. Winston Churchill, speaking not long ago at a meeting of English industrialists, said that parliamentary bodies are practically useless for dealing with economic questions and in that regard should be superseded. He goes further and says:
At this stage we ought to have the proper machinery for considering great economic issues.
He goes further and says:
I do not think party machinery is going to do the job well.
That is only too true. Coming from a man of such well known party inclinations and partisan views, his words bear some weight. Let me quote the views of another internationally known gentleman, Mr. Owen D. Young who, speaking at the Lotos club in New York, expressed similar doubts as to the efficacy of political mechanism in dealing with a world economically out of joint. He said:
That our politics and our economics are in conflict everywhere in the world to-day, he said, is due to the fact that economics are necessarily international, while politics are predominately national, and increasingly so in every country.
That point has been emphasized by other speakers. Apart altogether from the present depression through which we are passing, this so-called cyclical depression that has visited its evil on all the world, a type of depression that has visited this world four times, there having been two major and two minor ones during this short period, there has occurred on the North American continent a depression thirteen or fourteen times since constitutional government was established here. Apart altogether from that, you have the technological causes of unemployment and depression. The hon. member for Vancouver South (Mr. Mac-Innis) has dealt with that and I need not elaborate it except to point out to the leader of the government or whoever is taking his place, and the leader of the opposition, that in the last few years nearly three million people have been displaced by labour saving devices in the industries of the North American continent. Yet the inventive genius of man is not equal to the task of absorbing

1326	COMMONS
Economic Research-Mr. 'Garland (Bow River)
that enormous and steadily increasing number . of unemployed. Apparently we have nobody definitely committed to the task of studying that problem and finding out what the causes are and what the remedy may be.	*
If you want to find other things to examine into, I might submit the single problem that the problem of Canada is not the problem of India, the problem of India is not the problem of England, the problem of England is not the problem of Germany; but they are all inter-related in some way or other. The problem in India to-day is the problem of a deliberate policy of demonetizing silver-at appalling piece of fraudulent banking policy Which has brought disaster on all oriental countries, and even on countries in the southern parts of this continent, a policy which has had its effect on the export business of every country in the world that ever did business with the orient. I remember the Right Hon. Arthur Meighen, speaking not long ago before the Canadian Press convention in Toronto, where he pointed out very eloquently and clearly to the press men, and to the whole country, that the wealth of a thousand million people-think of it, Mr. Speaker-has been cut in two by a deliberate cold-blooded callous banking policy on the part of the British authorities in their endeavour to force India on to a gold basis. May I say to my hon. friend the Minister of Trade and Commerce (Mr. Stevens) that his former leader is strangely in discord with the views which he expressed earlier in this debate this afternoon. The minister of Trade and Commerce took issue with the hon. member for Red Deer (Mr. Speakman) upon the statement in the resolution to the effect that the problem of production had been largely solved, and he endeavoured to read into the resolution itself and into the utterances of the hon. member for Red Deer, an intention or an expression that was never at any time clear to anyone else in this house. The minister asked:	Would the hon. member have
industrial activity limit itself in its further progress? Surely no such intention has been expressed by any hon. member on this side of the house. Indeed, our whole hope is that we may be able to devise a distributive system that will absorb not only all that we produce, but all that we as human beings demand under modern standards of living. That is all we seek. The Right Hon. Arthur Meighen said in that speech to which I have just referred:

With a condition which approaches a superabundance of all things which should create happiness, thrift -would merely intensify the situation by lowering the consumption of commodities.
I submit that also to the leader of the government, who is an authority on thrift, for everybody else. Mr. Meighen said further:
Do not let us bow in eternal adulation of the leadership of those who have led us so far.
I wonder if he would like to come back some time. I wish he would.
Mr. LaVERGNE: I hope so.

subsubtopic: MOTION BY MR. SPEAKMAN PROPOSING ESTABLISHMENT OF NATIONAL COUNCIL TO STUDY SUBJECT
speechtext:
I do, too.
He was one of the finest debaters that ever stood in this house, and a man whose broadening views 'become apparent in utterances of -the type to which I have just referred. He says further:
How can we cure a condition of superabundance by refusing to absorb of that abundance? We just do not seem to be able to make available the surpluses of the world's goods which strike the eye at every turn.
I congratulate Mr. Meighen on his utterance, -and I submit that the Minister of Trade and Commerce might continue to follow in the footsteps of one whom he admired so intensely and so justly at one time.

subsubtopic: MOTION BY MR. SPEAKMAN PROPOSING ESTABLISHMENT OF NATIONAL COUNCIL TO STUDY SUBJECT
speechtext: I entirely concur in those views.

subsubtopic: MOTION BY MR. SPEAKMAN PROPOSING ESTABLISHMENT OF NATIONAL COUNCIL TO STUDY SUBJECT
speechtext:
I am glad
to hear that; I did not gather it from the hon. gentleman's speech. Dr. Jacks is a well-known economist, and I shall quote him because he presents, I submit, the condition in which this country and others now find themselves. My own words could not as adequately describe those conditions. Dr. Jacks says:
Whither mankind?

why are we asking this question to-day? I think we are doing so, not out of mere curiosity, but because we are getting anxious. We are not quite sure either where we are going or even where we are. We feel ourselves drifting-but whither? \Ve are like people on a great ship, full of treasure and of human life, which has lost its bearings in the night. The navigating officers are bewildered, the crew are getting mutinous, and the passengers, both first class and third, have got wind that something is wrong. Breakers ahead have been reported, and when we look over the side we see that -we are drifting. We are getting apprehensive about the future.
We have reason to be. Only the other day I heard one of the most eminent of living sociologists, Professor William MeDougall, say these words in public: "Western civilization is in imminent danger of collapse. Nothing but wise human effort guided by human science can prevent it collapsing." To which I would add

Economic Research-Mr. Garland (Bow River)
ray own belief that wise human effort, if it is sufficiently prompt, can prevent the catastrophe. Given that effort. I look with hope to the future: failing that effort, I feel sure we shall be on the rocks. We are drifting and there is a lee shore not far off.
No finer words could be used to describe the general economic and social conditions in. which this and other countries find themselves, and no better advice could be given to the government at the present time than to undertake now some definite planning for the future. But tjiey cannot plan, as the hon. member for Wetaskiwin (Mr. Irvine) so eloquently said, until they know what they are going to plan for; in fact, until they, know why the present conditions are.
What is the outlook, apart altogether from what Dr. Jacks has said? I take up a reputable paper, one to which even my hon. friends opposite can take no objection. Business Week, of New York, in a recent editorial said:
Business continues to crawl along the astonishingly flat trough that has lasted more than four months. Week to week, and even month to month, the movements are slight, sporadic, still insignifieent .... Moves for major international conference action to meet the emergency and check deflation are apparently at last developing around Governor Norman's visit, but further drift and delay are likely until a third winter of unemployment looms, so long as our official and financial economics emulates the ostrich, the original optimist.
The original optimist is particularly good. That is about all we have in this country, a lot of original optimists. They hope for the best without being willing even to look into conditions, much less to plan for a solution of them.

subsubtopic: MOTION BY MR. SPEAKMAN PROPOSING ESTABLISHMENT OF NATIONAL COUNCIL TO STUDY SUBJECT
speechtext:
Would it not be necessary before any such examination of economic conditions could be carried out, to make a very careful survey of the situation?
That survey is now being made through the census staff, as rapidly as it can be made.

subsubtopic: MOTION BY MR. SPEAKMAN PROPOSING ESTABLISHMENT OF NATIONAL COUNCIL TO STUDY SUBJECT
speechtext:
I submit
that in so far as the census staff this year has been committed for the first time to an examination as to the extent of unemployment and the causes for it, in so far as the individual is able to tell the census official-you go to the average man who is unemployed and he will tell you that he is unemployed but he cannot tell you the cause of his unemployment; who can?-

subsubtopic: MOTION BY MR. SPEAKMAN PROPOSING ESTABLISHMENT OF NATIONAL COUNCIL TO STUDY SUBJECT
speechtext:
There is not merely that, but the industrial investigations that accompany it.
22110-85}

subsubtopic: MOTION BY MR. SPEAKMAN PROPOSING ESTABLISHMENT OF NATIONAL COUNCIL TO STUDY SUBJECT
speechtext: All the information that can possibly be secured by these additional inquiries by the census takers this year is in large part already known to the government. The government has already made estimates of the number of unemployed in this country, and has made an estimate of the condition of industry in this country with a view to tariff action. I do not think we can afford to wait till after the census is taken before appointing a body such as is proposed in this resolution. My answer to the minister's question is that most of that information the government already has.

subsubtopic: MOTION BY MR. SPEAKMAN PROPOSING ESTABLISHMENT OF NATIONAL COUNCIL TO STUDY SUBJECT
speechtext:
We might wait
until after a tariff census before we undertake any increase in the tariff.

subsubtopic: MOTION BY MR. SPEAKMAN PROPOSING ESTABLISHMENT OF NATIONAL COUNCIL TO STUDY SUBJECT
speechtext:
That is
good. I wonder how that would suit hon. gentlemen opposite? I do not hear any loud approval, any strident applause or "hear, bear's" from those ranks at the present time.
In conclusion, I would ask the following question: If any one of the business men in this house, either to my right or opposite, were asked to go to a far distant country or far distant planet, if he could be sent there for the purpose of abolishing the insecurity of work, and if when he got there he found bursting granaries, fruits and vegetables rotting in the fields, farmers on the verge of bankruptcy, clothing factories, shoe factories and all kinds of factories either closed or working part time because those who needed the goods did not have the means to buy them, and those who were willing to produce the goods and ready to go to work could not be put to work; if he found outside the factories which were running on part time long lines of men poorly clad and under fed, workers simply begging for a chance to go back to work at pay requisite to keep themselves and their families from starvation; if finding that in the major part of the industrial centres he then visited the outskirts of the towns and discovered that in the most beautiful part of the country there were great, handsome, luxurious homes with attractive and spacious grounds and occupied by only a few people, a very small group in comparison with the total population-the owners of (be factories, the owners of the shops, the owners of the banks-living in mansions beyond the dreams of previous generations intent only upon enjoying life and devoted to the art of spending money, the art of wasting; if he found a small group, corresponding to the 603 people in Canada who pay income tax on
Privilege-Mr. Gobeil

850,000	a year or over, who were able to dispose of only a part of their incomes, and that the balance had to be put back into more industrial plants for the production of more goods which could not be bought by those who did the work of producing them,- if he found all that I wonder what hon. gentlemen would say about such an unsound condition of affairs. Yet a moment's reflection would show that that is exactly the position with which we are confronted to-day. In a sentence, we have six hungry men here and six loaves of bread there but we cannot introduce the loaves of bread to the hungry men.
Mr. LaVERGNE:	Was that not said on
the mountain about two thousand years ago?
